output_text:
Your mother, a 60-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital on 19/09/2022 and discharged on 19/10/2022, staying for a total of 1 month and 11 hours. She was admitted due to liver cirrhosis (permanent scarring of the liver), which had led to several serious complications. At the time of admission, she was experiencing septic shock (a life-threatening drop in blood pressure caused by a severe infection), acute respiratory failure (difficulty breathing requiring machine support), and reduced consciousness (obtunded state). Her blood tests showed a blood infection caused by Staphylococcus Aureus bacteria. She also had acute kidney injury (temporary kidney damage), which has since resolved. Other conditions present included pleural effusion (fluid around the lungs), ascites (fluid buildup in the belly), diabetes mellitus (sugar disease), systemic arterial hypertension (high blood pressure), non-toxic multinodular goiter (enlarged thyroid gland), anxiety and depression, spondyloarthrosis (spine joint wear), and a fibroadenoma (a benign breast nodule).

When she first arrived, her oxygen saturation was critically low at 85% (normal range is 95-100%), her blood glucose was high at 164 mg/dL (normal range is 70-100 mg/dL), and her serum albumin was low at 2.1 g/dL (normal range is 3.5-5.0 g/dL). Her INR (a measure of how long it takes blood to clot) was critically high at 4.4 (normal range is 0.8-1.2), indicating a high risk of bleeding. Her LDH (a liver enzyme) was 72 U/L, which is within the normal range of 140-280 U/L, though this value is often monitored in liver disease. Her folic acid level was low at 1.29 ng/mL (normal range is 3.37 ng/mL). Imaging showed bilateral pleural effusion (fluid on both sides of the lungs) and cardiomegaly (an enlarged heart). She also developed pressure injuries (bedsores) during her stay.

To treat these issues, several procedures were performed. On 18/09/2022, she underwent orotracheal intubation (a tube placed in the windpipe to help her breathe). She was successfully extubated (the tube was removed) on 03/10/2022. On 19/09/2022, a paracentesis (a procedure to drain fluid from the belly) and a thoracentesis (a procedure to drain fluid from around the lungs) were performed. Additional thoracentesis procedures were carried out on 23/09/2022, 06/10/2022, 10/10/2022, and 15/10/2022 to remove accumulated fluid. A transthoracic echocardiography (an ultrasound of the heart) and a POCUS (Point of Care Ultrasound) were also performed on 19/09/2022 to assess her heart and fluid levels.

She received several medications to manage her conditions. For her sugar, she was given Insulin NPH (to control blood sugar) at a dosage noted as 1008, and Glifage XR (Metformin) to control blood sugar, taken as 2 tablets at lunch and 2 tablets at dinner. To lower her cholesterol, she took Simvastatin 20 mg daily. For her high blood pressure, she took Losartan 50 mg, 1 tablet every 12 hours, and Hydrochlorothiazide, a water pill to reduce fluid, once a day. For her mental health, she was prescribed Sertraline 50 mg, 1 tablet every 12 hours, for depression and anxiety. For nerve pain, she took Gabapentin 300 mg daily. For bone health, she received Calcium and Vitamin D. Amitriptyline 25 mg was given for pain or sleep. Propranolol 10 mg every 12 hours was prescribed to protect against bleeding in liver disease. Omeprazole 40 mg was given to reduce stomach acid. To reduce fluid in the belly and lungs, she took Furosemide 40 mg twice a day and Spironolactone 50 mg daily. Antibiotics were used to treat the infection: Levofloxacin was started on 23/09 and stopped on 26/09; Oxacillin was started on 24/09 and stopped on 08/10; and Meropenem, a strong antibiotic for severe infection, was started on 27/09 and stopped on 08/10.

Going forward, her treatment plan includes adjusting the doses of her water pills (diuretics) while closely monitoring her kidney function. She will continue to receive care for her pressure injuries and will gradually wean off oxygen therapy. You must watch for warning signs such as signs of infection (fever, chills), worsening shortness of breath, bleeding (vomiting blood or black stools), confusion or drowsiness, and significant weight gain or swelling. A follow-up appointment with the Gastroenterology department (AGAF) is scheduled for 18/01. The family has been informed about the severity of her condition and the prognosis, and a shared decision was made not to perform new invasive measures.
